page.title: Test your idea on 100 customers
page.sub: The one prompt from the reel. Claude builds 100 buyers, pitches your idea to each one, and shows you who bought, who passed and why.
page.prompt_how: Paste this into Claude and fill in the three square brackets: your idea, who it's for and the price.
page.prompt_note: If the answer stops part-way through the table, type: continue.
page.tested_title: We ran it on a $39 snack box
page.tested_text: We ran this prompt on a $39-a-month healthy snack box for office workers. **19 bought and 81 passed.** The top reasons to pass were the price (24), an office that already has free snacks (15) and not being at a desk every day (13). The people most likely to buy were office managers spending company money, so the verdict was: don't sell it to individuals, test a team plan. **Not checked:** we ran it on a paid Claude plan, not the free one. Every name and quote in the reel is from that run.
page.tip: **The tip:** AI customers are nicer than real ones. Treat the result as the best case, then ask real people.

prompt: Act as a consumer panel for my business idea. My idea: [describe it in one sentence]. Who it's for: [your customer]. Price: [your price]. Step 1: invent 100 different buyers from that audience. Give each one a name, a monthly budget for this kind of thing, their habits, and one honest reason they might say no. Step 2: pitch my idea to every one of them. Each decides BUY or PASS, in their own words. Step 3: show me the full table of all 100, then a summary: how many bought, the top 5 reasons people passed with counts, the three buyer types most likely to buy, and the price at which most of them would say yes. Step 4: be tough, because real customers are less agreeable than AI ones. End with a verdict (worth testing on real people, or not yet) and the first real-world test I should run this week.

followups.label: Fix the top objection
followups.prompt: Take the number one reason people passed. Give me three ways to change the offer so it goes away, then re-run the same 100 buyers on the best one and show me what changed.
followups.note: Same panel, new offer, so you can see whether the change moved anyone.

followups.label: Find the right price
followups.prompt: Re-run the same 100 buyers at three prices: [low], [middle], [high]. Show how many buy at each and which price makes the most money.
followups.note: In our test, $39 got 19 buyers and $25 got 37.

followups.label: Write the pitch
followups.prompt: Write a 30-second pitch aimed only at the buyer type most likely to buy. Use their own words from the table.
followups.note: The table is full of phrases real customers might use. Borrow them.

checklist.title: Paste the prompt
checklist.detail: Fill in your idea, who it's for and the price.

checklist.title: Read who passed, and why
checklist.detail: The reasons people said no are worth more than the number who said yes.

checklist.title: Change one thing and run it again
checklist.detail: Use the three follow-ups: fix the top objection, test the price, write the pitch.

checklist.title: Ask real people
checklist.detail: Do the real-world test it gives you at the end, this week.

safety: **This is a rehearsal, not a forecast.** The buyers are made up by Claude, and AI customers are more agreeable than real ones.
**Don't spend money on the result alone.** Use it to find the objections, then test with real people.
